connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
disclosure_text: I am an immigrant who recently became a citizen to Canada. I immigrated in 2022 and completed my B.Ed this year and looking to contribute in Education sector of Ontario
micronarrative:
I immigrated to Canada in 2022, and I must say, the experience of navigating the immigration process was both challenging and rewarding. I worked very hard to get my degrees and gain the necessary work experience to score enough points in the Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) to secure a permanent residence. The idea of someone bypassing these processes and entering illegally just to take a spot that could have gone to someone who followed the rules seems unfair. 

Growing up in India, I witnessed the rise of islamophobia, which has been exacerbated by the government and some citizens. Many are looking to leave the country, but the procedure to do so must be followed. Settling illegally cannot be justified. 

Adapting to life in a new country has its own set of challenges. I had to slow down my speech and get used to the eurocentric pronunciation of vowels. My 'r's are still hard, and sometimes my 'a's are not as long as they should be. Interestingly, I've noticed that immigrants who arrived in their teenage years tend to maintain their native accent, while younger immigrants often adapt more quickly to the eurocentric accent. 

Despite the difficulties, I feel a strong sense of belonging in my new community. The journey has been tough, but it has also been an opportunity to grow and contribute to a new society.

reflexivity_response: My background as an immigrant and someone who has experienced starting over in a new country strongly shaped how I interpreted these posts. I tend to separate criticism of immigration policy, economics, or government systems from direct hate toward immigrants themselves. Because I have personally seen the financial, emotional, and professional struggles immigrants face, I often look for the underlying concern being expressed rather than immediately assuming malicious intent. For example, I know many immigrants work in labor-intensive jobs despite being highly educated because of barriers like credential recognition and financial pressures. That experience made me read some comments more as discussions about economics, fairness, or policy than direct attacks on immigrants. At the same time, I also recognize that certain phrases can carry hidden meanings or make immigrants feel unwelcome, especially when ideas about “who the country is for” are mentioned. My values around empathy, fairness, and lived experience likely made me focus more on context and intent rather than only the emotional impact of the wording.
